definition: Blockmodeling is a set or a coherent framework, that is used for analyzing social structure and also for setting procedure(s) for partitioning (clustering) social network's units (nodes, vertices, actors), based on specific patterns, which form a distinctive structure through interconnectivity.
details: It is primarily used in statistics, machine learning and network science. As an empirical procedure, blockmodeling assumes that all the units in a specific network can be grouped together to such extent to which they are equivalent. Regarding equivalency, it can be structural, regular or generalized. Using blockmodeling, a network can be analyzed using newly created blockmodels, which transforms large and complex network into a smaller and more comprehensible one. At the same time, the blockmodeling is used to operationalize social roles. While some contend that the blockmodeling is just clustering methods, Bonacich and McConaghy state that "it is a theoretically grounded and algebraic approach to the analysis of the structure of relations". Blockmodeling's unique ability lies in the fact that it considers the structure not just as a set of direct relations, but also takes into account all other possible compound relations that are based on the direct ones. The principles of blockmodeling were first introduced by Francois Lorrain and Harrison C. White in 1971. Blockmodeling is considered as "an important set of network analytic tools" as it deals with delineation of role structures

explainer.lead: Blockmodeling groups the actors in a social network according to how their relationships make them equivalent, then represents the ties between those groups as a smaller network. It helps reveal social roles and role structures that can be hard to see in a large web of individual connections.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a huge friendship map where you want to understand the groups and roles, not memorize every line. You put people with similar patterns of connections into teams, then draw a smaller map showing how those teams connect. This can show, for example, which groups connect internally and which groups link different parts of the network.
tiers.practitioner: Apply blockmodeling to network actors and their relations by choosing an equivalence notion—structural, regular, or generalized—and partitioning actors accordingly. Summarize relations within and between the resulting positions to obtain a blockmodel, and interpret it as a reduction of the network and an operationalization of roles. A key pitfall is treating it as generic similarity clustering: the analysis is relational, can include compound relations built from direct ties, and depends on the chosen equivalence.
tiers.paperLevel: For a network on vertices V with relations among them, blockmodeling seeks a partition of V into equivalent positions and represents the relations within and between those positions as a smaller blockmodel. Equivalence may be structural, regular, or generalized, and the framework considers compound relations based on direct relations as well as the direct relations themselves. Its principles were introduced by Francois Lorrain and Harrison C. White in 1971; the resulting interpretation depends on the equivalence used, while reduction to positions abstracts away individual-level detail.

explainer.example: Suppose eight employees form two departments of four, everyone has ties to all colleagues in their own department, and there are no ties between departments. Blockmodeling can group the employees into two department positions, producing a two-block model with a connected block inside each position and no connection between them. The eight-person network is then summarized by two positions and their internal and external relation patterns.

usedIn.name: Statistics
usedIn.detail: Used as an empirical procedure for grouping network units by relational equivalence.

usedIn.name: Machine learning
usedIn.detail: Supports relational clustering of network nodes into a compact structural representation.

usedIn.name: Network science
usedIn.detail: Reduces large, complex networks to smaller blockmodels that are easier to examine.

explainer.intuition: Instead of asking only who is connected to whom, blockmodeling asks which actors play equivalent relational roles. Grouping those actors into positions turns the detailed network into a compact map of relations between roles.
howItWorks: Start with a social network's actors and relations.
Choose structural, regular, or generalized equivalence.
Summarize ties within and between positions as blocks.
Interpret the reduced network and its role structure.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes large relational structures comprehensible without reducing them to isolated pairwise ties. Its blockmodels also provide a way to operationalize social roles and delineate role structures.
misconceptions: It is not merely clustering: it is a theoretically grounded, algebraic approach to relational structure.
It does not consider only direct ties; compound relations based on them also matter.
Equivalence is not a single rule: it can be structural, regular, or generalized.
